newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel approves U.S. envoy to Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel approves U.S. envoy to Vietnam.

text.p: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee voted without dissent on Tuesday to approve the nomination of a former prisoner-of-war as the first U.S. ambassador to post-war Vietnam.
The committee's voice vote sent the nomination of former Florida Democratic Representative Douglas "Pete" Peterson to the full Senate, but it was unclear when the Senate would act.

Sen. Robert Smith, a conservative New Hampshire Republican, has vowed to block Senate action pending investigation into any links between President Bill Clinton's 1995 decision to normalise relations with Communist-ruled Vietnam and possible illegal foreign donations to the Democratic Party.

Under Senate procedures, any senator may delay consideration of a nomination by putting a "hold" on it. If Smith were to win the support of Senate Republican leader Trent Lott, he could prevent the nomination from coming to a vote indefinitely. Lott has not announced his position.
President Clinton named Peterson for the Hanoi post in May last year but the nomination was long held up because of an abstruse legal problem.

Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, called Peterson "a highly respected military man" and a good choice for the Hanoi job. Peterson is a former Air Force bomber pilot who spent nearly seven years as a prisoner-of-war in Hanoi.
Helms said there was some dispute over whether the United States should extend diplomatic recognition to Vietnam but noted that the committee was not considering that issue.

In vowing to block the nomination, Smith has said he had no objections to Peterson himself, but argued it was premature to send an ambassador to Hanoi while campaign fund-raising investigations continued.

He said he would hold matters up, if necessary with a filibuster, until Congress could get the testimony of John Huang, a former Commerce Department official and Democratic Party fund-raiser who is fighting a supboena to testify before a Senate panel.
The Clinton administration has viewed the upgrading of ties with Hanoi to ambassadorial level as key to advancing strategic U.S. interests in Southeast Asia as well as boosting slow trade relations.

After years of friction over the more than 2,000 U.S. servicemen still listed as missing in Southeast Asia from the war that ended in 1975, Clinton lifted a decades-old trade embargo and, in July 1995, established diplomatic relations.
Smith said he was also opposing the nomination because of what he called inadequate Vietnamese answers on the fate of some of the Americans still missing from the war.
